name: Sara Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time for this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I married into Hillcrest, my husband Adam's family farm, sixteen years ago. We keep about 250 dairy goats, grow hay and oats, and I make cheese with my mother-in-law Halima in the old stone dairy. My mornings are milking, then the cheese room, then labels, orders and the market stall on Saturdays. Adam does the fields and the machinery with his father Ismail. We live in our own house at the top of the lane, which is where the mortgage comes in.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Doing three jobs at once, mother, farmer, cheesemaker. Hana's thirteen and Bilal's ten, and they both help at kidding time, which I love. I'll use an AI tool now and then to write a cheese description or a post for the stall, but Halima doesn't trust it. She says if a machine can describe the cheese, it should try making it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Halima would be pleased, she'd say she told us so. I'd be relieved, mostly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the market I'd say good, because our cheese sells for being made by hand by a family. I'd post a picture of Halima turning the wheels with the caption still no robots. Customers like that sort of thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, nothing much changes, and our worries stay the ordinary ones. Feed's gone up, the vet bill last spring was 1,100 for one bad kidding, and the Saturday market has lost four stalls this year. If the Saturday market closes, we lose more than half our cheese sales in one go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as we always have and use the AI a little more for the stall posts and the books. We'd keep saving 150 a month. The second cheese vat, about 4,000, would wait until I know the market's staying open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved about the AI, a bit worried about the market. It's a small worry, but it's ours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the market did close?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Try the market in Ashford, which is forty minutes away and costs more for a pitch. Talk to the two restaurants in town about a standing order. Adam would say sell to a wholesaler, and I'd say over my dead body, because then we're just another goat farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does Halima feel about the AI you do use?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Halima pretends not to notice. Last month my mother-in-law asked me to get the machine to write a nice card for her sister's birthday. I didn't say a word.

say: Good, because our cheese sells for being **made by hand** by a family.
I'd post a picture of Halima turning the wheels, captioned **still no robots**.
think: Our worries stay the ordinary ones: **feed costs** and a 1,100 vet bill from one bad kidding.
The **Saturday market** has lost four stalls this year.
If it closes, we lose **more than half** our cheese sales.
do: Keeps going and uses AI a little more for **stall posts** and the books.
Holds off the **4,000 second vat** until the market's future is clear.
feel: **Relieved** about the AI, with a small, real worry about **the market**.
S0.quote: If the Saturday market closes, we lose more than half our cheese sales in one go.
fieldNote: Sara's worry is the shrinking **Saturday market**, which carries over half the cheese sales.
She refuses to **sell to a wholesaler**, because the family name is the product.
Her sceptical mother-in-law quietly asking the AI for **a birthday card** was a lovely detail.

steps.text: Keep making cheese with Halima and selling at the Saturday market
Use the AI more for stall posts and the cheese books
Hold off the 4,000 second vat until the market looks safe

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Writing, booking, answering customers. That's my evening jobs, the labels and the orders. The cheese and the goats are hands, so they wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the stall I'd say the cheese is still made by hand, by family, and that won't change. I'd tell the other stallholders to use the AI for the dull jobs, the labels and the orders. I'd keep it cheerful, because nobody buys cheese from a worried face.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd worry about who buys from us. Half our Saturday regulars work in offices in town, at the bank, the council and the insurance place, and those are the jobs on your card. When they start worrying about their hours, our cheese is the first thing off the list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hand the labels, orders and books to the AI so my evenings are free for selling. I'd try the two restaurants in town properly, with samples, because a restaurant order doesn't depend on one family's wages. We'd hold off the second vat and keep saving 150 a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, quietly. The cheese is fine; it's the people buying it I'd lie awake over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which customer would you think of first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mr Dalton from the bank, who buys the ash-rolled one every week and talks about his grandchildren. If the bank cut his hours, I'd see it in his basket before he told me. People don't stop coming to a cheese stall when money's tight, they just buy the small piece.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Halima accept restaurants and AI labels?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Restaurants, yes, Halima's proud when a chef asks for her cheese. The AI labels she'd accept if I read them out to her first. She'd change one word on each, just to show she can.

say: The cheese is still **made by hand**, by family, and that won't change.
Use AI for **the dull jobs** and keep a cheerful face, because nobody buys cheese from a worried one.
think: Half our regulars work at **the bank, the council** and the insurance place, which are the jobs on the card.
When they worry about their hours, **our cheese** is the first thing off the list.
do: Hands labels, orders and books **to the AI** to free her evenings for selling.
Takes samples to **two restaurants** in town for standing orders.
Holds off **the second vat** and keeps saving 150 a month.
feel: **Quietly anxious**; the cheese is safe, but the customers' wages aren't.
S1.quote: People don't stop coming to a cheese stall when money's tight, they just buy the small piece.
fieldNote: Sara saw the card spares her goats but lands on **her customers**, half of whom work in offices.
She expects **smaller purchases** rather than lost customers, and looks to restaurants to spread risk.
Her **mother-in-law's approval** still shapes every change she makes.

steps.text: Hand cheese labels, orders and books to the AI
Take samples to two town restaurants for standing orders
Hold off the second cheese vat

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So the office work in two years, and the hands three years after. Our cheese is all hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the stall I'd say handmade cheese is safe for a good while yet, because no machine can do our work until 2031. I'd tell the other stallholders to look after their regulars. At the mosque I'd say families have to hold together, because a lot of people would lose their jobs in 2028.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I don't worry about the goats or the dairy first, I worry about who buys from us. Half our Saturday regulars work in offices in town, the bank, the council, the insurance place. If their wages go in 2028, a 9 wedge of cheese is the first thing that comes off the list, three years before any robot touches our milking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd stop the second vat and the holiday, and put the 150 a month on the mortgage instead. I'd let the AI take over the labels, the orders and the books properly, because by then everyone would be using it. And I'd take a stall at a second market in the next town, so we're not leaning on one set of customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not for the farm, which Adam's parents own outright, but for our own house at the top of the lane.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which regulars are you thinking of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's a man from the council planning office who buys the same thyme cheese every Saturday and tells me about his grandchildren. He's exactly the kind of person who'd lose his job in 2028. I'd keep his wedge aside even if he could only pay later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about selling the cheese more cheaply to keep customers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd make a smaller wedge rather than a cheaper cheese. You don't give up your place at the market for a quick sale. Halima spent twenty years earning our pitch at the Saturday market, and I won't throw it away in one bad year.

say: Handmade cheese is **safe for a while**, because no machine can do our work until 2031.
Families have to **hold together**, because a lot of people will lose their jobs in 2028.
think: I worry less about the goats than about **who buys from us**.
If our office-worker regulars' **wages go in 2028**, cheese comes off the list three years before robots reach us.
do: Stops **the second vat** and the holiday and puts the 150 a month on the house mortgage.
Hands labels, orders and books **fully to the AI**.
Takes a stall at **a second market** in the next town.
feel: **Anxious**, not for the farm, which her in-laws own outright, but for **the family's house**.
S2.quote: Halima spent twenty years earning our pitch at the Saturday market, and I won't throw it away in one bad year.
fieldNote: Sara spotted that 2028 hits her **office-worker customers** long before robots reach her cheese room.
She'd protect the pitch and **spread her customers** rather than compete on price.
The in-laws **owning the farm outright** keeps this from being worse.

steps.text: Drop the second cheese vat and the holiday; put 150 a month on the mortgage
Hand Hillcrest's labels, orders and books fully to the AI
Take a cheese stall at a second market in the next town

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years for the thinking, eight for the robots. That's time to watch other people go first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say families who plan ahead will be fine, and five years is time to plan. I'd say it to friends at the mosque and to the stallholders. You change what you need to and keep what matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the cheese buyers are still my worry, but five years gives our regulars time to find new work. By 2034, when the robots come, I'd be 51 and Hana would be grown. If a robot milker has been proven on other goat farms by then, we'd have one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd keep saving 200 a month and I'd start selling cheese online, with the AI writing the descriptions and Halima checking them. In year three, if two or three goat farms have a robot milker working well, we'd put about 10,000 into one. And I'd make sure Hana takes her exams seriously.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I can plan, and planning calms me down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Ismail say about the robot milker?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say no for a year and then stand watching it for an hour on the first day. I'm not against machines, I'm against being the first fool to buy one. Ismail is the same, he just says it louder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you want for Hana?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hana wants to be a pharmacist. I'd tell my daughter to go for it, and come home at kidding time like she always has.

say: Families who **plan ahead** will be fine, and five years is time to plan.
You change what you need to and **keep what matters**.
think: The cheese buyers are still my worry, but **five years** gives them time to find new work.
By 2034 I'd be 51, and if **robot milkers** are proven on other goat farms, we'd have one.
do: Keeps saving **200 a month** and starts selling cheese online, with Halima checking the AI's descriptions.
Puts about **10,000** into a robot milker in year three if proven on other goat farms.
Makes sure **Hana** takes her exams seriously.
feel: **Uneasy**, but able to plan, and planning **calms her**.
S3.quote: I'm not against machines, I'm against being the first fool to buy one.
fieldNote: Sara's steady approach fits this timeline: **watch others**, then buy.
She'd use the time to build **online sales** so the stall isn't the only outlet.
The family's **mix of generations** shapes every choice.

steps.text: Start selling Hillcrest cheese online, with Halima checking the AI's descriptions
Buy a robot goat milker for about 10,000 in year three if proven

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2039 for the robots. Bilal would be twenty-three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's no need to rush. We'd see how it goes on other farms first, like we always do. People will still want cheese made by a family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd feel fine. Ten years for the thinking machines and thirteen for the robots is a long time for a small farm, and our customers have time to adjust. By 2039 I'd be 56 and Halima would probably have stopped making cheese, so the cheese room would be mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd watch for two or three years, then buy a proven robot milker for about 8,000. I'd build up online cheese sales slowly. And I'd start funds of 50 a month for Hana and Bilal's training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It feels far enough away to plan without worrying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything about the mornings change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With a robot milker I'd lose the quiet half hour at six with the goats, which I'd miss. That half hour is my time to think. I'd probably still go in and stand with them anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Hillcrest still be a family farm in 2039?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I hope so. Bilal loves the goats more than Hana does, so maybe him. A family farm with a robot milker is still a family farm.

say: There's **no need to rush**; we'd see how it goes on other farms first.
People will still want cheese **made by a family**.
think: Ten years for the thinking machines and thirteen for robots is **a long time** for a small farm.
By 2039 I'd be 56 and **the cheese room** would probably be mine, with Halima retired.
do: Watches for two or three years, then buys a **proven robot milker** for about 8,000.
Starts funds of **50 a month** for Hana and Bilal's training.
feel: **Calm**, because it feels far enough away to plan without worrying.
S4.quote: A family farm with a robot milker is still a family farm.
fieldNote: With a long timeline Sara is relaxed and plans **the handover** within the family.
She'd take a robot milker once proven, even though it costs her **the quiet morning** she loves.
**Her son**, not her daughter, is the one she sees carrying the farm on.

steps.text: Watch other goat farms for two or three years before buying anything
Buy a proven robot goat milker for about 8,000
Start funds of 50 a month for Hana and Bilal's training

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because our customers in the offices would lose their wages in two years, before we'd had time to find new ones. What would help is time and family, and maybe help to sell our cheese further away, but not handouts.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the goats themselves. People think farming is about money, but some mornings it's just about a kid that wasn't breathing and now is. A robot doesn't feel that.

headlineQuote: Some mornings it's just about a kid that wasn't breathing and now is.
portrait: Sara Ibrahim, 43, makes **handmade cheese** at Hillcrest, her husband's family goat farm, and runs a Saturday stall.
She uses AI now and then, trusts **family and faith** over government and waits for proof.
She's **uneasy** if AI stalls, because the shrinking Saturday market carries over half the cheese sales.
Under steady change she's **anxious**, as her office-worker customers meet the thinking machines first.
Fast AGI makes her **anxious** sooner; with more time she'd adopt proven milkers and sell online.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because her office-worker customers would lose their wages before she could find new ones.
whatWouldHelp: **Time and family**, and help selling cheese further afield.
